journeyIntro: For people sharing love and everyday life. Practise speaking openly, handling disagreements and staying close.

lessons.title: A Softer Start
lessons.summary: Bring up the little things without blame.

steps.title: The first line sets the tone
steps.body: How a conversation begins often decides how it ends. Open with blame and your partner is busy defending themselves before they’ve even heard the request.

steps.title: Try a soft start-up
steps.body: Say what happened, how it left you feeling and what you’d like. “The sink’s full and I’m wiped out. Could you do the dishes tonight?”

steps.prompt: Your partner has left the dinner dishes again and you’re exhausted. Which opening is most likely to get help?

options.text: “You never help with anything.”
options.why: “Never” turns one evening into a verdict on them, so they defend themselves instead of helping.

options.text: “I’m wiped out and the sink’s full. Could you take the dishes tonight?”
options.why: It names the situation and your need, and gives them something easy to say yes to.

options.text: Wash everything in silence and stew about it.
options.why: It keeps the peace tonight, but resentment builds and they have no idea anything’s wrong.

steps.prompt: Swap blame for a feeling.
steps.after: when the dishes pile up after dinner.
steps.why: It describes your state without guessing at their motives, which keeps the door open.

steps.prompt: When something small bugs you at home, what do you usually do first?
steps.reply: Knowing your habit helps you catch it next time and reach for a softer opening.

steps.prompt: Harsh start or soft start?

cards.text: “You never think about anyone but yourself.”
“I’m feeling stretched. Could we split tonight’s jobs?”
“Can I ask for something small that would really help?”

steps.why: A soft start names your feeling and asks for something specific; a harsh one attacks, and the talk goes downhill from there.

steps.body: Next time something small bothers you, start with what happened and what you’d like, not what they “always” do.

lessons.title: Hear the Feeling
lessons.summary: Listen for what matters beneath the words.

steps.title: Facts on top, feelings underneath
steps.body: When your partner vents about their day, the details matter less than how it left them feeling. That’s the part they most want you to catch.

steps.prompt: Your partner walks in and says, “Today was a nightmare.” What’s the best first response?

options.text: “That sounds exhausting. Want to tell me about it?”
options.why: It names the feeling and invites them in, without steering the conversation anywhere.

options.text: “Mine was worse, honestly.”
options.why: Comparing days turns their moment into a contest, and they’re likely to stop sharing.

options.text: “Well, at least it’s over now.”
options.why: Meant kindly, but it hurries past the feeling before they’ve had a chance to say it.

steps.title: Name it, then wait
steps.body: Offer a feeling word: “frustrating”, “lonely”, “a lot”. If you guess wrong they’ll correct you, and that still helps them feel heard.

steps.prompt: Reflect the feeling back.
steps.before: It sounds like today was really
steps.why: A guess at their feeling shows you’re tuned in; the other two judge it or shrink it.

steps.prompt: When your partner is upset, what’s your first instinct?
steps.reply: Every one of those comes from care. Leading with listening just helps the rest land better.

steps.title: A cancelled birthday

lines.text: My sister just cancelled my birthday dinner. Again.

steps.prompt: What do you send back?

options.text: Don’t let it get to you, she’s always been like that.
options.why: It brushes the hurt aside, so they’re left feeling it alone.

options.text: Oh love, that really stings, especially three years in a row. I’m sorry. 💛
options.reaction: It really does. Thank you for getting it.
options.why: You named the feeling and why it makes sense, which is what helps someone feel heard.

options.text: Want me to book somewhere for just us two instead?
options.reaction: Maybe… I’m still just annoyed though.
options.why: A kind idea, but jumping to fix it skips the part where they feel understood.

steps.body: Tonight, when your partner tells you about their day, name the feeling you hear before offering anything else.

steps.title: Small bids, big signals
steps.body: “Look at that!” “Guess what happened?” These little invitations are called bids. How you answer them, day after day, shapes how close you feel.

steps.title: Three ways to answer
steps.body: You can turn towards a bid (respond), turn away (miss it) or turn against it (snap). Turning towards often takes just a few seconds.

steps.prompt: On a walk, your partner points out a ridiculous-looking bird. Which response turns towards the bid?

options.text: Keep scrolling and say, “Mm-hm.”
options.why: One missed bid feels tiny, but lots of them add up to feeling alone together.

options.text: “Take a photo, I’ll look later.”
options.why: It postpones the moment, and by later the shared fun of it has gone.

options.text: Stop, look and laugh: “It looks so grumpy!”
options.why: A few seconds of shared attention tells them their small moments matter to you.

steps.prompt: Which bids from your partner are easiest for you to miss?
steps.reply: Spotting your blind spot makes those bids much easier to catch this week.

steps.prompt: Match each bid with a way to turn towards it.

pairs.a: A sigh while reading the news
A funny meme sent at lunch
pairs.b: A reply that shows you laughed

steps.why: Bids are small reaches for attention. Turning towards them, even briefly, is what builds closeness over time.

steps.body: Notice the small bids your partner makes today, and turn towards at least three of them.

lessons.title: Say What You Need
lessons.summary: Make room for closeness and personal space.

steps.title: Needing space isn’t rejection
steps.body: Wanting quiet after a long day doesn’t mean you love your partner any less. Saying so clearly protects both your energy and your closeness.

steps.prompt: You’re drained and need quiet, but your partner wants to talk the moment you get home. What helps most?

options.text: Push through the chat while getting more irritable.
options.why: They’ll feel the irritation without knowing why, and the chat goes worse for you both.

options.text: Head to another room without a word.
options.why: Silence leaves them guessing, and many people read it as you being upset with them.

options.text: “I want to hear it. Can I have 20 minutes to recharge first?”
options.why: It shows you care, names your need and gives a clear time, so it doesn’t feel like a brush-off.

steps.title: Add a bridge back
steps.body: The kindest boundaries come with a plan to reconnect: “I need an hour to myself, then let’s cook together.” Space feels safer when it has an end.

steps.prompt: Add the bridge back.
steps.why: It pairs your need with a promise to return, so your partner feels included, not shut out.

steps.prompt: What do you need more of at home, and how could you ask for it?
Asking for quiet time. Put these in order.
steps.why: Spotting it early lets you ask calmly; a time limit and a plan to reconnect show it’s about rest, not distance.

steps.body: Name one need to your partner today, and say when you’ll reconnect afterwards.

lessons.title: Build Everyday Trust
lessons.summary: Let reliability grow through small promises.

steps.title: Trust grows in small deposits
steps.body: Trust comes less from grand gestures and more from ordinary reliability: being where you said, doing what you said and owning it when you don’t.

steps.prompt: You promised to book the dentist for you both, then forgot. Your partner asks about it. What builds trust?

options.text: “It’s not a big deal, it can wait.”
options.why: It may feel small to you, but brushing it off tells them their reminders don’t count.

options.text: “I forgot, I’m sorry. I’ll book it on my lunch break today.”
options.why: Owning it and naming a specific fix shows you can be relied on, even when you slip.

options.text: “The booking site wasn’t working.”
options.why: Small excuses feel harmless, but if they’re found out, trust takes a much bigger hit.

steps.prompt: Make a promise you can keep.
steps.why: Specific and realistic beats vague or over-ambitious, and it’s easy to see you did it.

steps.title: Trust is never about fear
steps.body: Healthy relationships never involve fear, control or harm. If something in yours feels unsafe, talking to someone you trust or a local support line can help.

steps.prompt: Which kind of promise do you find hardest to keep?
steps.reply: That’s a good place to start: one smaller, clearer promise in that area builds trust fastest.

steps.prompt: Builds trust or chips away at it?

cards.text: Doing what you said, even small things
“I’ll do it later” that never happens
Telling them early when plans change
Hiding a small purchase to avoid a talk
Owning it when you get it wrong

steps.why: Trust grows from many small moments of keeping your word and being honest, especially when it’s awkward.

steps.body: Keep one small promise today exactly as you said, or give an honest update before it’s due.

lessons.title: Pause the Argument
lessons.summary: Cool down without abandoning the conversation.

steps.title: When the heat takes over
steps.body: In a heated argument your heart races and listening gets harder. Pushing on rarely helps; a short, agreed pause usually does.

steps.prompt: You’re arguing about money and your voices are rising. What’s the most helpful move?

options.text: “I’m getting worked up. Can we take 20 minutes and come back?”
options.why: It owns your state, sets a time and promises to return, so it’s a pause rather than an escape.

options.text: Walk out and say you’re done talking about it.
options.why: Leaving with no return time can feel like abandonment, and the issue stays unsolved.

options.text: Keep arguing until one of you gives in.
options.why: Someone may give in, but nobody feels understood, and the same fight tends to come back.

steps.title: Use the break well
steps.body: Do something calming, like a walk or some music, rather than replaying the argument in your head. Then come back when you said you would.

steps.prompt: Make the pause feel safe.
words: come back to it at eight
steps.answer: come back to it at eight
steps.why: A set time reassures your partner the conversation matters and isn’t being dodged.

steps.prompt: When an argument heats up, what do you tend to do?
steps.reply: Each of those is a way of coping. An agreed pause gives you something better to reach for.

steps.prompt: Taking a time-out in a fight. Put these in order.
steps.why: A pause only helps if you ask for it kindly and return; calming your body first lets you actually hear each other.

steps.body: While you’re both calm, agree a pause signal with your partner and how long a break should last.

lessons.title: Repair After a Slip
lessons.summary: An apology can open a door to repair.

steps.title: Everyone snaps sometimes
steps.body: Strong couples aren’t the ones who never hurt each other. They’re the ones who notice it and repair it, quickly and sincerely.

steps.prompt: You snapped at your partner after a stressful commute. A little later, what repairs it best?

options.text: “Sorry, but you were winding me up.”
options.why: The “but” cancels the apology and hands the blame straight back to them.

options.text: Be extra nice all evening and never mention it.
options.why: Kindness helps, but without words the hurt can linger, unspoken, between you.

options.text: “I was sharp with you earlier. I’m sorry, you didn’t deserve that.”
options.why: It names exactly what you did and takes responsibility, which makes it easy to accept.

steps.title: What makes an apology land
steps.body: Name what you did, own the impact and skip the excuses. You can add what you’ll try next time. Short and specific beats long and dramatic.

steps.prompt: Own the impact.
steps.after: I’ll try to pause next time.
steps.why: It owns the effect on them. Excuses, even true ones, make an apology feel half-hearted.

steps.prompt: What makes apologising hardest for you?
steps.reply: Completely human. A short, specific apology is enough, and it gets easier every time.

steps.title: The night out

lines.text: Can I say something? You were on your phone most of my friend’s dinner.
I felt a bit on my own tonight.

steps.prompt: How do you reply?

options.text: I was only checking work stuff for a minute.
options.reaction: It was more than a minute 😕
options.why: Defending the detail misses how they felt, so the hurt stays open.

options.text: Well, your friends aren’t easy to talk to.
options.why: Turning it back on them makes it a new argument instead of a repair.

options.text: You’re right, I was distracted. I’m sorry you felt alone. Can we try again next time?
options.reaction: Thanks for hearing me. Yes, let’s 💛
options.why: You owned it, named their feeling and offered to do better, which is what makes a repair land.

steps.body: Think of a recent sharp moment and offer your partner a short, specific apology, with no “but”.

lessons.title: Share the Load
lessons.summary: Talk fairly about invisible household work.

steps.title: The work nobody sees
steps.body: Remembering birthdays, planning meals, noticing the milk’s running low: this “mental load” is real work, and carrying it alone breeds resentment.

steps.title: Own it, don’t just help
steps.body: Helping when asked still leaves one person managing everything. Owning a task means you notice it, plan it and finish it, without reminders.

steps.prompt: Your partner seems stressed juggling meals, bills and appointments. What helps most?

options.text: Ask which jobs feel heaviest and take full ownership of one or two.
options.why: Owning a task from start to finish lifts the planning burden, not just the doing.

options.text: Ask them to give you a list of what to do.
options.why: Kind, but they still have to notice, plan and hand out jobs, which is the tiring part.

options.text: Point out that you both work hard, so it’s even.
options.why: It skips past how they actually feel, and they may stop raising it altogether.

steps.prompt: Offer real ownership.
steps.why: A clearly owned job takes the remembering off their plate, not just the errand.

steps.prompt: Which household job could you fully own, from start to finish?
Match each vague ask with a clear one.

pairs.b: “Could you do the bins on Tuesdays?”
“Could you do two school runs a week?”

steps.why: Vague asks sound like criticism and are hard to act on; clear ones say exactly what would help.

steps.body: Pick one recurring job and own it this week, from noticing it’s needed to getting it done, without a reminder.

steps.title: The stories we tell ourselves
steps.body: When a partner seems distant, our minds rush to explain it, often with the worst version. Curiosity checks the story before you believe it.

steps.prompt: Your partner has been quieter than usual all week. What’s the most trusting next step?

options.text: Decide they’re annoyed with you and go quiet too.
options.why: Acting on a guess can create the very distance you were worried about.

options.text: “You’ve seemed quiet lately. How are you doing?”
options.why: It shares what you’ve noticed without blame and lets them tell you what’s really going on.

options.text: Look through their phone to find out why.
options.why: Checking in secret damages trust far more than one quiet week ever could.

steps.title: Notice, ask, then listen
steps.body: Share what you’ve seen, ask an open question, then really listen. If they’re not ready to talk, let them know you’re around when they are.

steps.prompt: Ask, don’t accuse.
steps.why: Describing what you see invites an answer; the others assume a reason and spark a defence.

steps.prompt: When your partner seems off, what does your mind jump to first?
steps.reply: Whatever your mind jumps to, it’s only a guess until you ask them.

steps.title: Something on their mind

lines.text: Nothing bad! Just something that’s been on my mind.

steps.prompt: What do you send?

options.text: Of course. Thanks for telling me. I’ll make tea and we can talk after dinner. ☕
options.why: You stay calm, thank them and make space, which makes it easy for them to open up.

options.text: That sounds ominous… what did I do?
options.reaction: Nothing! Honestly, it’s not about you.
options.why: Jumping to the worst makes it about you and can make them wary of raising things.

options.text: Can’t you just tell me now?
options.reaction: I’d rather talk properly, in person.
options.why: Pushing for it now ignores the way they asked to have the talk.

steps.body: Check in about one change you’ve noticed in your partner, describing what you saw rather than what you assumed.

lessons.title: Choose Us Again
lessons.summary: Create a small ritual that lasts.

steps.title: Love needs regular tending
steps.body: Busy weeks can quietly turn partners into flatmates. Closeness rarely fixes itself; it grows back through small moments you choose on purpose.

steps.prompt: Work and life have left you both feeling disconnected. What’s the best first step?

options.text: Wait for your next holiday to reconnect.
options.why: Holidays help, but months of distance before then can make the gap feel wider.

options.text: Suggest ten phone-free minutes together every evening.
options.why: Small, regular rituals are easier to keep than big plans, and they add up quickly.

options.text: Assume real love shouldn’t take any effort.
options.why: Every lasting relationship takes effort; needing it is a sign of care, not of trouble.

steps.title: Make it a ritual
steps.body: Morning coffee together, a Sunday walk, a goodnight check-in. The best rituals are short, regular and something you both look forward to.

steps.prompt: When do you feel most connected to your partner?
steps.reply: That’s your starting point. Build a small ritual around it and protect it in your week.

steps.prompt: What small ritual could you two start this week?
Brings you closer or lets you drift?

cards.text: A phone-free dinner once a week
Talking only about chores and bills
Asking, “What’s been on your mind lately?”
A six-second hug when you get home

steps.why: Closeness comes back through small, regular rituals of attention, not just big gestures or holidays.

steps.body: Suggest one small weekly ritual to your partner and put the first one in both your diaries.
